planting.note: Plant divisions or potted crowns in fall into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in dappled to partial shade; the clump resents disturbance and may sulk for a season before settling in.

directions: Paeonia japonica is a true woodland peony native to mountain forests of Japan and Korea, forming a tidy clump of glossy, blue-green, deeply divided foliage that emerges reddish in spring. In mid-spring it opens pure white, single, bowl-shaped flowers with a central boss of golden stamens, followed in summer by showy seed pods that split to reveal glossy blue-black fertile seeds beside bright red infertile ones. Unlike border peonies it thrives in the filtered light of a deciduous canopy and resents hot, exposed sites. Grow in rich, humusy, well-drained soil and leave undisturbed once established, as it is slow to recover from transplanting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted crowns in fall into rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade, mimicking the understory of its native West China forests; mulch over winter in colder zones.

directions: Paeonia mairei is a woodland species peony from the forests of Sichuan and Yunnan, valued for its dusky rose-pink to magenta single flowers held above handsome, deeply cut, matte-green foliage in mid-spring. The nodding, bowl-shaped blooms give way by late summer to striking seed pods that open to display shiny black and coral-red seeds against the split scarlet husk. It grows naturally beneath open forest canopy and performs best with the dappled light and leafy, humus-rich soil of a shaded border rather than full sun. Once established the clump is long-lived and needs little more than an annual mulch of leaf mold.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall into humus-rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil in partial to full shade; colonies spread gradually and are best left undisturbed once sited.

directions: Anemone trifolia is a European woodland anemone closely related to the familiar A. nemorosa but readily distinguished by its three-parted, trifoliate leaves and slightly larger white flowers that open in early spring before the deciduous canopy fills in. Each wiry stem carries a single star-shaped bloom with a central tuft of pale stamens, and the foliage dies back to a creeping rhizome by midsummer as the plant goes dormant. It spreads slowly into drifts in cool, humus-rich soil under beech or oak woodland, making it a good companion for hepatica and early woodland bulbs. Give it light shade and consistent moisture in spring, tolerating drier summer dormancy once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions or root cuttings in spring into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade with some sun; give it plenty of room, as established colonies spread by vigorous rhizomes.

directions: Macleaya microcarpa is a statuesque Chinese woodland-edge perennial grown for its bold, deeply lobed, blue-green leaves with pale undersides and its towering plumes of small coral-pink to buff flowers held well above the foliage in summer. It tolerates the light shade of a woodland margin better than most tall border perennials, bringing architectural height and airy texture to a partly shaded bed. The vigorous rhizomatous roots spread readily, so site it where it can be allowed to naturalize or confine it with a barrier in smaller gardens. Cut stems ooze an orange-yellow sap and the foliage has a soft, felted texture that contrasts well with bold hostas and ferns.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into deep, moisture-retentive, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; the clump is extremely slow from seed and best started from division of an established crown.

directions: Veratrum oxysepalum is a bold Japanese woodland species prized for its broad, pleated, glossy leaves that emerge like furled umbrellas in spring and form a striking architectural clump before the flower spike develops. In mid-to-late summer it sends up dense, branched racemes of star-shaped, greenish-white to cream flowers that age to a soft green, held well above the basal foliage. It thrives in the cool, consistently moist soil and filtered light of a mountain forest understory, and resents hot, dry summer conditions. All parts of the plant are highly toxic if ingested, so site it away from grazing animals and curious pets.
